p.s: What if I told you that a king, a real-life emperor, held up the collapsed roof of a wrecked train car with his bare shoulders to save his family?
This isn't a scene from a Marvel movie.
This isn't a myth.
This is the incredible, almost forgotten true story of Alexander the Third. The last giant to sit on the Russian throne.
A man of immense strength, who could reportedly bend silver coins with his fingers.
But on one fateful autumn day in 1888, his strength wasn't a party trick.
It was the only thing standing between his entire family and a gruesome death.
To understand what happened on that train, you first need to understand the man.
Alexander the Third was never supposed to be Tsar.
He was the second son, living in the shadow of his brilliant older brother, Nicholas.
Alexander was trained for the military, not for ruling the largest empire on Earth.
He was known for his bluntness, his quiet nature, and his intimidating physical presence.
Standing at 6 feet 3 inches, or 190 centimeters, he was a giant for his time.
But fate had other plans.
His brother died suddenly, and Alexander was thrust into the spotlight, inheriting a vast, turbulent empire plagued by revolutionaries and political intrigue.
Unlike many rulers of his time, he was a devoted family man.
His marriage to the Danish princess Dagmar, who became Empress Maria Feodorovna, was a genuine love story.
He cherished his quiet family life above all the pomp and ceremony of the court.
For his children, including the young Nicholas—the future and final Tsar of Russia—he was simply 'Papa'.
He was called 'The Peacemaker' because Russia didn't fight a single major war during his reign.
But the greatest battle of his life wouldn't be on a field of war.
It would be inside a twisted metal death trap.
In October 1888, the imperial family was heading home to St. Petersburg after a vacation in Crimea.
They traveled in the Imperial Train.
And you need to understand, this wasn't just a train.
It was a rolling palace.
A 19th-century Air Force One.
It had luxurious sleeping cars, offices, a kitchen that could rival any palace, and a magnificent dining car decorated with leather and fine wood.
It was the pinnacle of luxury and technology.
A golden cage on wheels.
But the foundation of that luxury was weak.
Russia's railway network had expanded rapidly, but often with corruption and cutting corners.
The tracks were often flimsy, laid on sand instead of proper gravel, unable to support heavy, high-speed trains.
The Imperial Train was notoriously heavy.
And to make up for delays, the driver was often ordered to go faster than was safe.
On this particular trip, two powerful steam engines were attached to pull the train at high speed, a direct violation of safety regulations.
A young, ambitious railway manager named Sergei Witte had personally warned the government about the dangers months earlier.
He pointed out that the combination of heavy cars, high speed, and weak tracks was a recipe for disaster.
He was ignored.
His concerns were dismissed as alarmism.

As the family sat down for lunch in the dining car on October 29th, cruising at nearly 70 kilometers per hour, they had no idea they were hurtling towards a catastrophe that had already been predicted.
The moment came without warning.
A violent jolt threw everyone from their seats.
A second, more powerful impact, and the world dissolved into a nightmare of splintering wood, shattering glass, and twisted metal.
The dining car was torn apart.
The heavy wheels broke through the floor, and the walls collapsed inward.
The roof buckled, crashing down on the terrified passengers.
Total darkness.
The air filled with dust, the screams of the injured, and the smell of hot metal.
The Tsar's children were screaming.
His wife was trapped.
And the roof was still caving in.
In that moment of pure chaos, Alexander acted.
Pinned by the debris, bruised and battered, he found his footing.
With a primal roar, he straightened up, pushing his immense shoulders against the collapsing roof.

Eyewitnesses, his own family included, would later recount the unbelievable sight: the Emperor of Russia, standing amidst the wreckage, holding up a roof that weighed thousands of pounds, creating just enough space for his wife and children to crawl out from under the debris.
He held it long enough for his family to escape to safety.
Only then did he let go, the structure groaning as it settled.
But his work wasn't done.
Emerging from the wreckage, his clothes torn, covered in dirt and blood, Alexander didn't behave like a victim.
He behaved like a commander.
He ignored his own injuries—severe bruises and what would later be diagnosed as kidney damage—and began personally directing the rescue operations.
He helped pull servants, guards, and officials from the twisted remains of other cars.
He comforted the dying and organized aid for the wounded using the first-aid kits from the train's doctor.
The scene was horrific.
21 people were dead.
Dozens more were severely injured.
But the entire Imperial family had survived.
It was declared a miracle.
But was it?
An investigation was immediately launched.
The government, desperate to avoid blame, initially pushed the narrative of a terrorist bomb.
It was a familiar story in an era of revolutionary violence.
But Sergei Witte, the same man who had warned of the danger, was part of the investigation team.
And he wasn't buying it.
He knew the truth was far more mundane and far more damning.
It wasn't a bomb.
It was negligence. Greed. Corruption. The state of the railway was the real culprit.
Witte's investigation proved that the train had derailed simply because it was going too fast on poorly maintained tracks.
It was a disaster caused not by enemies of the state, but by the state itself.
In the end, a few officials were dismissed, but the real issues were swept under the rug.
The story of the 'miraculous escape' was far better for propaganda than the story of criminal incompetence.
The Borki train disaster became a defining moment for Alexander the Third.
The public saw him as a hero, a true 'Tsar-Batyushka' or 'Father-Tsar', who physically protected his people—and his family.
Churches were built on the site to commemorate the 'miracle'.
But the event left deep scars, both visible and invisible.
Alexander suffered from constant back pain for the rest of his life.
The doctors believed the immense physical strain of lifting the roof caused catastrophic damage to his kidneys.
His health began to decline steadily.
Just six years later, in 1894, Alexander the Third died of kidney disease.
He was only 49 years old.
Many historians believe the 'miracle' at Borki ultimately cost him his life.
The psychological impact on the witnesses was also profound.
The young Tsarevich Nicholas, who saw the horror up close, would inherit the throne far sooner than anyone expected.
Was his view of the empire, and its stability, forever shaken by the knowledge that it could all collapse in an instant?
In a way, the image of Alexander the Third holding up the roof of that train car is a powerful metaphor for his entire reign.
He was a force of nature, single-handedly holding together a vast, crumbling empire through sheer will and strength.

s.emphasis: But once he was gone, the roof came crashing down for good.

p.s: The story of Borki is more than just a tale of incredible survival.
It's a story of courage, of failure, and a chilling foreshadowing of the even greater crash that was coming for the Russian Empire.
What do you think?
Could this single event have changed the course of Russian history by shortening the life of its last powerful Tsar?
